prompt: Each scenario below shows a form of intelligence at work. Name whether it demonstrates Animal, Human, or Artificial intelligence.

cases.text: Pacific salmon navigate thousands of kilometres back to the exact stream where they hatched to spawn.
cases.explanation: Instinctual survival and navigation behavior built into the species is animal intelligence.

cases.text: A radiology system scans chest X-rays to highlight suspicious lung nodules before a doctor reviews the file.
cases.explanation: Object detection in medical imaging is a core capability of artificial intelligence.

cases.text: A composer writes an original cello score to capture the grief of a character in a dramatic film scene.
cases.explanation: Creativity and emotional understanding in composing music are hallmarks of human intelligence.

cases.text: An e-commerce tool reads ten thousand French product reviews, translates them into English, and flags angry customers.
cases.explanation: Language translation and sentiment analysis performed by machines are artificial intelligence tasks.

cases.text: Young beavers that have never seen a dam before gather branches and mud to block running water.
cases.explanation: Building shelter and structures from instinct for survival is animal intelligence.

cases.text: A streaming app studies the episodes you finished this month and queues three new shows that match your listening habits.
cases.explanation: Pattern recognition in historical listening data to power a recommendation engine is artificial intelligence.

prompt: Sort each development into the force driving the 21st-century rise of Machine Learning that it illustrates.

cards.text: Specialized graphics processors run millions of matrix calculations in parallel, cutting training time from months to hours.
cards.explanation: Faster parallel processors directly represent the increase in compute power.

cards.text: Millions of household smart meters, phones, and checkout scanners stream continuous records every second.
cards.explanation: Connected devices and digital transactions generate the explosion of Big Data needed to train ML models.

cards.text: A retailer keeps ten years of item-level receipt histories on cloud drives for a few cents per gigabyte.
cards.explanation: Cheaper disk and cloud storage make it affordable to retain massive historical datasets.

cards.text: Modern server racks pack thousands of times more floating-point operations per second than 1990s workstations.
cards.explanation: Exponential growth in processing speed is the increase in compute power.

cards.text: Every search query, video pause, and cart addition across billions of web sessions is logged as a training example.
cards.explanation: Vast streams of user interactions expand the volume of Big Data available for learning.

cards.text: A hospital network archives millions of high-resolution MRI scans without deleting older years to free up space.
cards.explanation: Falling storage costs allow organizations to keep large unstructured archives indefinitely.

prompt: Each team below is choosing a machine learning algorithm. Name whether the task fits a Decision Tree, Linear Regression, or Logistic Regression.

cases.text: A grocery chain wants to predict the exact number of coffee bags a store will sell next week at different shelf prices.
cases.explanation: Predicting a continuous numerical quantity (sales volume from price) is a Linear Regression task.

cases.text: An online clothing shop wants to predict whether a subscriber will click the link in a promotional email (yes or no).
cases.explanation: Predicting a binary outcome (click vs. no click) from customer and product characteristics uses Logistic Regression.

cases.text: A park ranger checks trail conditions step by step—first whether there is lightning, then whether the trail is icy—to decide whether to open the hike.
cases.explanation: Splitting a decision into sequential condition branches (like checking weather conditions to play tennis) is a Decision Tree.

cases.text: A dealership estimates the dollar resale value of a used van based on its mileage and age.
cases.explanation: Dollar resale value is a continuous outcome, which Linear Regression predicts.

cases.text: A travel website predicts whether a visitor viewing a hotel page will book the room or leave without booking.
cases.explanation: Book vs. not book is a binary outcome ideal for Logistic Regression.

prompt: Match each core element of Random Forest with how it works when a logistics firm predicts package delivery delays.

pairs.match: Instead of relying on one decision tree, the firm builds hundreds of trees, each trained on a random sample of past shipments and route features.
pairs.explanation: Ensemble Method builds a forest of decision trees trained on random subsets of data and features.

pairs.match: Because each tree sees different routes and weather columns, one tree catches port bottlenecks while another catches winter storm patterns.
pairs.explanation: Independent training on random subsets creates diverse models that capture different patterns.

pairs.match: To classify a parcel as Late or On-Time, the system picks whichever class most trees voted for; to estimate minutes delayed, it averages all trees' numbers.
pairs.explanation: Classification takes the majority vote across trees, while regression takes the average prediction.

pairs.match: A single tree that memorized a freak one-day highway closure is outvoted by the rest of the forest, preventing overfitting on new shipments.
pairs.explanation: Combining many independent trees cancels out individual errors and reduces overfitting.

prompt: Sort each data characteristic, task, or evaluation metric into Supervised Learning or Unsupervised Learning.

cards.text: Training examples pair every input record with a known output target.
cards.explanation: Supervised learning requires labeled data where inputs are paired with known outputs.

cards.text: Prediction errors are corrected directly against ground-truth labels during training.
cards.explanation: Supervised learning uses direct feedback from labels to correct errors.

cards.text: Evaluated with Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, or RMSE.
cards.explanation: These metrics compare model predictions against known true labels or values.

cards.text: The algorithm receives only input variables with no predefined outcomes or target column.
cards.explanation: Unsupervised learning analyzes unlabeled data containing inputs only.

cards.text: Used for K-Means clustering, topic modeling (LDA), and dimensionality reduction (PCA).
cards.explanation: Clustering and dimensionality reduction discover hidden structure without labels.

cards.text: Assessed with the Silhouette Score, Elbow Method, or Reconstruction Error.
cards.explanation: Without ground-truth labels, unsupervised models use internal structure metrics like Silhouette Score and Elbow Method.

question_text: A pharmacy chain launches two analytics projects: Project A uses five years of labeled prescription refill records (refilled on time vs. abandoned) to predict which patients will miss their next refill. Project B feeds 40 unlabeled store-level demographic and basket variables into an algorithm to group its 600 pharmacies into natural store formats. Which learning paradigms do Projects A and B use?
hint: Check whether each project trains on known historical outcomes (labels) or searches for natural groupings without prior labels.
correct_answer_citation: Supervised Learning: Algorithms learn from labeled data, where each input example is paired with a corresponding output (target). Unsupervised Learning: Algorithms analyze unlabeled data to discover hidden patterns, groupings, or structures without predefined outcomes.

options.option_text: Project A uses Supervised Learning (classification from labeled refill outcomes); Project B uses Unsupervised Learning (clustering unlabeled stores).
options.option_explanation: Correct. Project A maps inputs to a known historical target label (refilled vs. abandoned), while Project B discovers natural clusters in unlabeled store data.

options.option_text: Project A uses Unsupervised Learning because future refills have not happened yet; Project B uses Supervised Learning because store variables are numerical.
options.option_explanation: Predicting future outcomes from labeled historical records is Supervised Learning, and numerical inputs without target labels are still Unsupervised.

options.option_text: Both projects use Supervised Learning because both rely on historical pharmacy data stored in a structured database.
options.option_explanation: Having historical data in a database does not make a task supervised; what matters is whether the training data include known output labels.

options.option_text: Both projects use Unsupervised Learning because neither project uses a rules-based expert system.
options.option_explanation: Both Supervised and Unsupervised Learning are machine learning paradigms, distinguished by the presence or absence of training labels.
